name: Beard growth serum / Kirkland minox foam

card.summary: Over-the-counter 5% minoxidil foam, often a store-brand like Kirkland, used off-label on the beard; the only active ingredient with trial evidence for beard growth.
card.aka: Kirkland minoxidil foam, Rogaine foam, beard serum
card.note: Off-label for beard use; effects reportedly reverse when stopped; beard "serums" vary in ingredients.

quick.overview:
Minoxidil is an over-the-counter topical sold for scalp hair loss, and 5% foam products, including store brands, are widely discussed for beard growth. Commercial beard "serums" are a separate and varied category.

Small randomized trials of minoxidil lotion for beard enhancement exist, and Wikipedia lists beard growth as an off-label use.
quick.mechanism: Minoxidil is a prodrug converted in follicles to minoxidil sulfate, an ATP-sensitive potassium channel opener; proposed hair effects include increased blood flow and growth-factor induction.
quick.risks: Topical use can cause itching, irritation and dandruff; hypertrichosis (unwanted hair growth) is described, and benefits reverse when use stops.

lead: Beard growth serum, in looksmaxxing usage, covers two things: commercial beard serums with varied ingredient lists, and over-the-counter 5% minoxidil foam, including store brands such as Kirkland, used on the face. People use them to fill patchy areas, thicken a sparse beard and add density along the cheeks and jawline, which frames the face and can make the jaw look stronger.[1][2]

Minoxidil topical foam and solution are sold over the counter in the US for androgenetic alopecia, with the 5% foam approved in 2006 and generics following in 2017.[1] Beard growth is described on Wikipedia as an off-label use, and the article cites studies of minoxidil for facial hair enhancement, including in transgender men.[1] Wikipedia notes that beard growth begins at puberty and is driven by dihydrotestosterone and inherited traits, which is why some people have sparse or patchy beards.[3]
Commercial beard serums are marketed under many brand names; the contents differ by product, and no studies found address them as a class.

chain: Minoxidil foam or a beard serum is applied to the beard area
Follicles are proposed to stay longer in the growth phase and produce thicker hairs
Denser, fuller beard coverage while use continues
angle.text: People apply 5% minoxidil foam to patchy or sparse beard areas to build density, which gives a fuller jawline and cheek line. Randomized trials of minoxidil for beard enhancement have been published, and results are reported to reverse after stopping.[1]

paras: Minoxidil is a prodrug whose active metabolite, minoxidil sulfate, is formed mainly by SULT1A1 in follicles.[1] It is an ATP-sensitive potassium channel opener, and proposed effects include greater blood supply to follicles, increased growth factors such as VEGF, HGF and IGF-1, and keeping follicles in the growth (anagen) phase.[1] Topical absorption is only about 1.2 to 1.4 percent.[1]

Topical use can cause itching, irritation, dandruff and unwanted hair growth elsewhere on the body, and temporary shedding is listed as an adverse effect.[1] Hair benefits require continued use; for the scalp, density returns to roughly placebo levels about 24 weeks after stopping.[1]

Upjohn developed the compound in the late 1950s and 1960s; the hair-growth effect was found in 1971 after oral minoxidil was developed for blood pressure.[1] Topical minoxidil was approved as Rogaine in 1988 and became OTC in 1996.[1]
Store-brand 5% foam is discussed as a lower-cost version of the same active ingredient. Beard serums sold under brand names vary in what they contain.

A randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled study of 3% minoxidil lotion for beard enhancement was published in the Journal of Dermatology in 2016, and a randomized trial of 3% topical minoxidil for facial hair enhancement in transgender men was published in 2026. Wikipedia also lists beard growth, including studies in transgender men, as an off-label use.[1]

timeline.event: Researchers find that minoxidil causes hair growth.[1]
Topical minoxidil (Rogaine) approved for male baldness.[1]
